title: Permission Groups Discovery
summary: Permission groups discovery is the mapping step an intruder performs after gaining a foothold, and its value is prioritisation rather than access. Every environment organises rights into groups, so enumerating those groups and their members tells the attacker which accounts are worth chasing and which machines are worth holding. The behaviour appears in three scopes, which is why the technique is split into sub-techniques for local groups, directory domain groups, and cloud identity groups. Local discovery reads the account database on one host, domain discovery queries a central directory over the network, and cloud discovery calls a provider identity interface for roles, policies, and object access control lists. In practice an attacker rarely types one command by hand. Automated collection tools walk the directory, resolve nested group membership, and produce a graph of who can reach what, which is why the volume and shape of the queries matter more than any single command. Detection therefore compares two things. First, the process and command telemetry that shows a group listing utility running where no administrator is working, ideally through process creation events such as Windows Security 4688 or Sysmon 1. Second, the directory side, where a sudden burst of lightweight protocol queries from one internal host to a domain controller, or a new identity calling role and policy listing actions in a cloud tenant, separates reconnaissance from the steady background of legitimate inventory and helpdesk activity.

beginner.definition: A group is a list of accounts that share the same rights. This technique is an attacker reading those lists. They want to know which accounts hold more power than others. The same idea applies to groups on one computer, in a company directory, and in a cloud platform.
beginner.whyItMatters: Knowing who has power tells an attacker where to aim next. They can target a specific person instead of guessing. They can also learn which machines are most valuable. On its own this activity changes nothing, so it is easy to dismiss. That is exactly why it is worth noticing early.
howItWorks: The attacker lists the groups that exist on the computer they have already reached.
They list the members of those groups, looking for administrator accounts.
They query the company directory for domain wide groups and their members.
They read the shared company directory over the network, which leaves queries in its logs.
In cloud environments they call the identity interface for roles, policies and access lists.
Automated tools repeat these steps at scale and build a map of who can reach what.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital at night. A stranger in the corridor stops at the staff board beside the nurses' station. The board shows who is on duty, who carries the medicine cabinet key and who can open the drug store. He reads it, memorises three names and walks on. He has not opened a single door, yet he now knows exactly which people to follow. Group discovery is reading that staff board.
takeaways: Listing groups changes nothing by itself, so it is easy to overlook.
Unexpected group listing commands on a workstation are worth investigating.
Directory query volume from one internal host often reveals automated collection.

objectives: Explain why an attacker maps permission groups after gaining access.
Describe the differences between local, domain and cloud group discovery.
Identify the process creation and directory logs that record this activity.
Explain how automated collection tools differ from a single command in the telemetry.
Recognise legitimate inventory and helpdesk activity that can look the same.
